messages:
maria: heads-up — ALB started deregistering ~30% of targets in the edge pool (us-west-2) around 14:22 UTC. Targets marked unhealthy with repeated healthcheck timeouts.

dev-oncall: @maria can you paste a few ALB healthcheck log lines / error codes? any common source IPs?

maria: pasted snippets: `ELB healthcheck -> 504` and `target response timeout`. From inside cluster curl to pod IP: `curl -sv http://10.244.5.12:8080/health` returns 200 quickly. ALB logs show TCP timeout/back-to-back retries. Node kernel logs show `nf_conntrack: allocation failed` and nat port allocation retries.

samir: that smells like SNAT/ephemeral port exhaustion — ALB health checks hit the node IPs and responses are SNAT'd back; if conntrack table or ephemeral ports are exhausted you get timeouts.

ari: did we change any SNAT or kube-proxy settings during last deploy? I landed a kube-proxy tweak earlier but only in staging.

devon: I actually rolled a kube-proxy iptables rule tweak in edge region yesterday (13:50) to reduce conntrack timeout for CLOSE_WAIT. Could be related but not sure.

maria: interesting — also seeing `source port reuse` patterns in nat logs (same src port used across many connections), which suggests port pool shrinking or aggressive reuse.

ben: quick mitigation suggestions: 1) temporarily loosen ALB healthcheck sensitivity (increase timeout/interval), 2) scale up nodes to reduce per-node SNAT pressure, 3) if using aws-cni, add more IPs per ENI / assign secondary IPs.

opsbot: deploy-bot: incident ticket created: EDGE-LB-2026-045 (paging eng-oncall).

dev-oncall: I'm going to try a low-risk mitigation first: increase target group health check interval to 30s and timeout to 5s, roll it for one ALB. If flapping stops we know it's transient. Also will flip one node pool to enable more IPs/ENIs.

maria: running a curl from ALB vantage is hard (can't ssh from ELB), but I ran `socat` proxy from a jump to emulate health checks — reproduced the timeout when source ports are saturated.

samir: long-term we should avoid heavy SNAT for node IPs: either use target type=instance for ALB (so traffic hits node networking without SNAT) or enable AWS CNI externalSNAT/hostport options for healthchecks. Both have tradeoffs.

devon: quick config we can try on the deployment to reduce probe flaps (in case backend is slow during GC):

```
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 3
```
I'll bump `timeoutSeconds` to 5 and `failureThreshold` to 5 for the edge pool as a temp measure.

ari: also check kube-proxy conntrack sysctls: `net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max` and `nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established`. If they're low we'll see allocations fail under burst.

maria: implementing scale-up (+3 nodes) now and updating healthcheck interval. I'll monitor ALB target states and conntrack metrics. Opening a ticket with AWS about ALB healthcheck connection churn and ephemeral IP reuse.

dev-oncall: sounds good. Please post metrics: per-node `conntrack_count`, `ephemeral_ports_used`, ALB 5xx/504s.

maria: will share a graph in ~10m. current plan: ramp scale, relax healthchecks, revert kube-proxy change if we confirm causality.

samir: if we get repeated incidents we should consider changing target type to instance for this pool and evaluate cost/ops impact.

dev-oncall: thanks all — keep updates here. :thumbsup:
